title: Geometry
summary: Similar triangles and Pythagoras, area formulas (Heron, shoelace, sine), circle theorems and power of a point, coordinate geometry, and volume and surface area of solids.

concepts.title: Similar triangles and the Pythagorean theorem
concepts.body:
Two triangles are similar when their angles match exactly. Then each side of one triangle is the same multiple (the scale factor) of the matching side in the other, so the ratios of matching sides are all equal. The most useful source of similar triangles is a line drawn parallel to one side. It cuts off a small triangle whose angles copy the big triangle's angles, so its sides are a fixed fraction of the big triangle's sides.

For right triangles, the Pythagorean theorem $a^2+b^2=c^2$ links the two legs $a$ and $b$ with the hypotenuse $c$. The converse is also true: if $a^2+b^2=c^2$, the angle opposite $c$ is a right angle. Drop an altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse and you get two smaller right triangles, each similar to the original. This gives $h^2=pq$, where $h$ is the altitude and $p,q$ are the two pieces of the hypotenuse. For example, in a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle the altitude to the hypotenuse is $\frac{3\cdot 4}{5}=\frac{12}{5}$.
keyFacts: $a^2+b^2=c^2$ for a right triangle with hypotenuse $c$
Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides
concepts.whenToUse: A line parallel to one side of a triangle, a right triangle with a perpendicular drawn to its hypotenuse, or any length question about a right triangle.

concepts.title: Area: base-height, sine, Heron and shoelace
concepts.body:
Every area formula reads the same quantity from different information. The base-height formula $\frac12 bh$ is the starting point: any side can be the base, and the height is the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the line of that base. If you know two sides $b$ and $c$ and the angle $A$ between them, drop an altitude onto $b$. Its length is $c\sin A$, so the area is $\frac12 bc\sin A$. This works even when the triangle is not right, because the altitude always exists.

If you know all three sides, Heron's formula $K=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$, with $s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$, gives the area without any angle. It comes from the base-height formula after the altitude is eliminated with the Pythagorean theorem. When the vertices are given as coordinates, the shoelace formula is easier. Multiply each $x$ by the next $y$, subtract the product of the next $x$ and the current $y$, add the results around the polygon, and halve the absolute value. It works for any simple polygon because it adds up signed trapezoid areas.

For example, the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(0,3)$ has the terms $0\cdot 0-4\cdot 0=0$, $4\cdot 3-0\cdot 0=12$, and $0\cdot 0-0\cdot 3=0$. Their sum is $12$, so the area is $6$, which matches $\frac12\cdot 4\cdot 3$.
keyFacts: Triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of their bases
concepts.whenToUse: Two sides with the angle between them, all three sides, or vertices given as coordinates. Pick the formula that matches the data you are given.

concepts.title: Circle theorems and power of a point
concepts.body:
Circle theorems turn angle questions into arc questions. A central angle equals the arc it cuts off, and an inscribed angle (its vertex on the circle) is half of that arc. This is why every angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. Two inscribed angles on the same arc are equal, and opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and the two tangent segments from an outside point have equal length.

When two chords cross inside a circle, the angle between them is half the sum of the arc it cuts off and the arc of its vertical angle. The reason is that this angle is an exterior angle of a triangle, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote angles. Each remote angle is an inscribed angle, so each is half an arc.

Power of a point connects lengths. For a point $P$ outside a circle, any line through $P$ meets the circle at two points $A$ and $B$, and the product $PA\cdot PB$ is the same for every such line. It also equals $PT^2$, where $PT$ is the length of a tangent from $P$. For example, if a secant has $PA=4$ and $PB=9$, a tangent from $P$ has length $\sqrt{36}=6$.
keyFacts: Central angle equals its arc; inscribed angle is half its arc
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$
Power of a point: $PA\cdot PB=PT^2$ for a secant and a tangent from $P$
concepts.whenToUse: Circles with chords, secants or tangents, especially when a tangent length or a product of segments from an outside point is asked for.

concepts.title: Coordinate geometry
concepts.body:
Coordinates turn a picture into arithmetic. For points $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$, the distance is $\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$. This is just Pythagoras applied to the horizontal and vertical gaps. The midpoint is the average of the coordinates. A line can be written $y=mx+c$, where $m$ is the slope (rise over run). Two lines are perpendicular exactly when their slopes multiply to $-1$, because turning a line of slope $m$ through a right angle gives slope $-\frac1m$.

To find where two lines meet, set their equations equal. For instance, $3x=7-\frac x2$ gives $\frac72 x=7$, so $x=2$ and $y=6$. A line crosses the $x$-axis where $y=0$. Once the vertices are known, the shoelace formula gives the area. A triangle with a horizontal base has area $\frac12\cdot\text{base}\cdot\text{height}$, where the height is the vertical gap from the apex to the base line.

Reflection is a useful tool. The reflection $Q$ of a point $P$ across a line is the same distance from the line as $P$, on the other side. The segment $PQ$ is perpendicular to the line, and the line passes through the midpoint of $PQ$. Those two facts pin down $Q$ without a formula.
keyFacts: Reflection $Q$ of $P$: $PQ$ is perpendicular to the mirror and its midpoint lies on the mirror
concepts.whenToUse: Problems that give points or lines as coordinates, or ask for intersections, perpendiculars, reflections or areas of regions in the plane.

concepts.title: Volume and surface area of solids
concepts.body:
Volume measures how much space a solid fills, and surface area measures the total area of its outside. For a prism or cylinder, every horizontal slice is a copy of the base, so $V=Bh$, where $B$ is the base area and $h$ is the height. For a pyramid or cone, the slices shrink toward the apex. A slice at a fraction $t$ of the height above the base has area $(1-t)^2 B$, because its linear size is $1-t$ of the base. Adding up all the slices gives one third of the prism's volume, so $V=\frac13 Bh$.

Scaling is the key shortcut for solids. If every length is multiplied by $k$, areas are multiplied by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$. So a plane cutting a cone parallel to its base at half the height leaves a small cone with $\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac18$ of the original volume.

Spheres and cones need a little more. A ball of radius $r$ has $V=\frac43\pi r^3$ and $S=4\pi r^2$. When a ball touches the faces of a solid, its centre is at distance $r$ from each face. A cross-section through the centre often turns the 3D problem into a circle inscribed in a triangle. The lateral surface of a cone unrolls into a sector of radius $\ell$ (the slant height) whose arc has length $2\pi r$, so its area is $\pi r\ell$, and the total surface area is $\pi r^2+\pi r\ell$.
keyFacts: Cone: $S=\pi r^2+\pi r\ell$ with slant height $\ell$
Scaling all lengths by $k$ multiplies areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$
concepts.whenToUse: Any problem about a solid that is cut, stacked, scaled, or has a ball or cone inside or on top of it.

workedExamples.title: Altitude to the hypotenuse
workedExamples.problem: In right triangle $ABC$, the right angle is at $C$, with $AC=9$ and $BC=12$. Let $H$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the hypotenuse $AB$. What is the length of $CH$?
steps: Compute the area with the legs as base and height: $\frac12\cdot 9\cdot 12=54$.
Compute the same area with $AB$ as base and $CH$ as height: $\frac12\cdot 15\cdot CH$.
Set the two expressions equal: $\frac12\cdot 15\cdot CH=54$, so $CH=\frac{108}{15}=\frac{36}{5}$.
workedExamples.takeaway: The altitude to the hypotenuse equals the product of the legs divided by the hypotenuse, because the area can be computed two ways.
workedExamples.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
import math
# C=(0,0), A=(0,9), B=(12,0): right angle at C, AC = 9, BC = 12
A = (0, 9); B = (12, 0); C = (0, 0)
dx, dy = B[0] - A[0], B[1] - A[1]
AB2 = dx*dx + dy*dy
AB = math.isqrt(AB2); assert AB*AB == AB2      # hypotenuse 15
cross = dx*(C[1] - A[1]) - dy*(C[0] - A[0])    # signed twice-area of ABC
print(F(abs(cross), AB))                       # distance from C to line AB

workedExamples.title: Area from three sides
workedExamples.problem: A triangle has side lengths $7$, $15$, and $20$. What is its area?
workedExamples.takeaway: Heron's formula needs only the three sides, and checking whether the product is a perfect square keeps the arithmetic clean.
workedExamples.verify:
import math
# B=(0,0), C=(15,0); A=(x,y) with AB = 7 and AC = 20
x = (7*7 - 20*20 + 15*15) / (2*15)     # -4.2
y = math.sqrt(7*7 - x*x)               # 5.6
area = 0.5 * 15 * y
assert abs(area - 42) < 1e-9
assert abs(math.hypot(x - 15, y) - 20) < 1e-9   # AC really is 20
print(round(area))

workedExamples.title: Tangent from a secant
workedExamples.problem: A point $P$ lies outside a circle. A line through $P$ meets the circle at $A$ and then at $B$, with $PA=4$ and $AB=5$. A tangent from $P$ touches the circle at $T$. What is $PT$?
steps: The secant runs from $P$ through $A$ to $B$, so $PB=PA+AB=4+5=9$.
Power of a point: the square of the tangent equals the product of the whole secant and its outside part, so $PT^2=PA\cdot PB=4\cdot 9=36$.
Sanity check: $PT$ is the geometric mean of $PA$ and $PB$, so it must lie between them, and $4<6<9$.
workedExamples.takeaway: A tangent length squared equals the product of the two secant segments from the outside point.
workedExamples.verify:
import math
# P = (0,0); the secant is the x-axis, meeting the circle at A = (4,0) and B = (9,0)
O = (6.5, 2.0)                          # centre lies above the midpoint of AB
r2 = (4 - O[0])**2 + (0 - O[1])**2
assert abs((9 - O[0])**2 + (0 - O[1])**2 - r2) < 1e-9   # B is on the circle
PT = math.sqrt((O[0]**2 + O[1]**2) - r2)                # tangent length from P
print(round(PT))

problems.problem: A ladder $13$ metres long leans against a vertical wall. Its foot rests on level ground $5$ metres from the base of the wall. How many metres up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?
problems.hint: The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right triangle. Which side is the hypotenuse?
problems.solution: The ladder is the hypotenuse, $13$, and the distance from the wall to the foot is a leg, $5$. The height $h$ satisfies $h^2=13^2-5^2=169-25=144$, so $h=12$.
problems.verify:
hits = [h for h in range(0, 100) if 5*5 + h*h == 13*13]
print(hits[0])

problems.problem: In triangle $ABC$, point $D$ lies on side $AB$ with $AD=4$ and $DB=6$. Point $E$ lies on side $AC$ so that segment $DE$ is parallel to $BC$, and $DE=5$. What is the length of $BC$?
problems.hint: Parallel lines create similar triangles. Compare $AD$ with the whole side $AB$.
problems.solution: Since $DE\parallel BC$, triangles $ADE$ and $ABC$ are similar. Their ratio is $\frac{AD}{AB}=\frac{4}{10}=\frac25$, so $\frac{DE}{BC}=\frac25$. Hence $BC=\frac{DE}{2/5}=\frac{5}{2/5}=\frac{25}{2}$.
problems.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
A = (F(0), F(0)); B = (F(10), F(0)); C = (F(3), F(4))   # AB = 10
D = (F(4), F(0))                                          # AD = 4
t = (D[0] - A[0]) / (B[0] - A[0])                         # AD/AB = 2/5
E = (A[0] + t*(C[0] - A[0]), A[1] + t*(C[1] - A[1]))      # E on AC with AE/AC = 2/5
def d2(P, Q):
    return (P[0] - Q[0])**2 + (P[1] - Q[1])**2
assert d2(D, E) * 25 == d2(B, C) * 4                      # DE/BC = 2/5 for this shape
print(F(5) / t)                                           # BC = DE / (2/5)

problems.problem: Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A=(1,2)$, $B=(7,2)$, and $C=(4,9)$ in the coordinate plane. What is its area?
problems.hint: Pick $AB$ as the base. How far is $C$ from the horizontal line through $A$ and $B$?
problems.solution: Side $AB$ is horizontal with length $7-1=6$. The vertex $C$ is $9-2=7$ units above that line, so the area is $\frac12\cdot 6\cdot 7=21$. The shoelace formula gives the same value.
problems.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
pts = [(1, 2), (7, 2), (4, 9)]
s = 0
for i in range(len(pts)):
    x1, y1 = pts[i]
    x2, y2 = pts[(i + 1) % len(pts)]
    s += x1*y2 - x2*y1
print(F(abs(s), 2))

problems.problem: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$ and $AC=12$, and the area of the triangle is $24$. What is $\sin A$, where $A$ is the angle at vertex $A$?
problems.hint: The formula $\frac12 bc\sin A$ uses exactly the two sides that meet at $A$.
problems.solution: Using the two sides that meet at $A$, the area is $\frac12\cdot AB\cdot AC\cdot\sin A=\frac12\cdot 8\cdot 12\cdot\sin A=48\sin A$. Setting this equal to $24$ gives $\sin A=\frac12$.
problems.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
AB, AC, K = 8, 12, 24
# A=(0,0), B=(AB,0), C=(x,y) with |AC| = 12; area = (1/2)*AB*|y|
y = F(2*K, AB)                 # height of C above AB = 6
assert AC*AC - y*y > 0        # such a C exists
print(y / AC)                  # sin A = height / AC

problems.problem: Quadrilateral $PQRS$ has vertices $P=(0,0)$, $Q=(5,1)$, $R=(8,6)$, and $S=(2,4)$, listed in order around its boundary. What is its area?
problems.hint: Use the shoelace formula on the four vertices in order. Do not forget the factor $\frac12$.
problems.solution: The edge terms $x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i$ are $0$, $5\cdot 6-8\cdot 1=22$, $8\cdot 4-2\cdot 6=20$, and $2\cdot 0-0\cdot 4=0$. They sum to $42$, so the area is $\frac12\cdot 42=21$.
problems.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
pts = [(0, 0), (5, 1), (8, 6), (2, 4)]
s = 0
for i in range(len(pts)):
    x1, y1 = pts[i]
    x2, y2 = pts[(i + 1) % len(pts)]
    s += x1*y2 - x2*y1
print(F(abs(s), 2))

problems.problem: What is the area of a triangle whose three side lengths are $11$, $13$, and $20$?
problems.hint: Heron's formula needs the semiperimeter $s$. Check whether $s$, $s-a$, $s-b$ and $s-c$ give a perfect square product.
problems.solution: The semiperimeter is $s=\frac{11+13+20}{2}=22$. Then $s-11=11$, $s-13=9$, $s-20=2$, so the area is $\sqrt{22\cdot 11\cdot 9\cdot 2}=\sqrt{4356}=66$.
problems.verify:
import math
# B=(0,0), C=(20,0), A=(x,y) with AB = 13 and AC = 11
x = (13*13 - 11*11 + 20*20) / (2*20)     # 11.2
y = math.sqrt(13*13 - x*x)               # 6.6
area = 0.5 * 20 * y
assert abs(area - 66) < 1e-9
assert abs(math.hypot(x - 20, y) - 11) < 1e-9   # AC really is 11
print(round(area))

problems.problem: Four distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on a circle, in that order around the circle. The arc from $A$ to $B$ that does not contain $C$ or $D$ measures $80$ degrees, and the arc from $C$ to $D$ that does not contain $A$ or $B$ measures $40$ degrees. The chords $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $P$ inside the circle. What is the measure of $\angle APB$, in degrees?
problems.hint: The angle between two crossing chords is half the sum of the two arcs it cuts off, one on each side of the crossing.
problems.solution: $\angle APB$ is an exterior angle of triangle $PBC$, so it equals $\angle PBC+\angle PCB$. The angle $\angle PBC$ is the inscribed angle $\angle DBC$, which intercepts arc $CD$ of $40^\circ$, so it is $20^\circ$. The angle $\angle PCB$ is the inscribed angle $\angle ACB$, which intercepts arc $AB$ of $80^\circ$, so it is $40^\circ$. Therefore $\angle APB=60^\circ$.
problems.verify:
import math
def pt(deg):
    t = math.radians(deg)
    return (math.cos(t), math.sin(t))
A, B, C, D = pt(0), pt(80), pt(180), pt(220)   # arc AB = 80, arc CD = 40
def cross(u, v):
    return u[0]*v[1] - u[1]*v[0]
r = (C[0] - A[0], C[1] - A[1])     # direction of chord AC
s = (D[0] - B[0], D[1] - B[1])     # direction of chord BD
qp = (B[0] - A[0], B[1] - A[1])
u = cross(qp, s) / cross(r, s)
P = (A[0] + u*r[0], A[1] + u*r[1])  # crossing point of the two chords
va = (A[0] - P[0], A[1] - P[1])
vb = (B[0] - P[0], B[1] - P[1])
cosang = (va[0]*vb[0] + va[1]*vb[1]) / (math.hypot(*va) * math.hypot(*vb))
print(round(math.degrees(math.acos(cosang))))

problems.problem: A point $P$ lies outside a circle. One line through $P$ meets the circle at $A$ and at $B$, where $A$ is closer to $P$, with $PA=5$ and $AB=7$. A second line through $P$ meets the circle at $C$ and $D$, where $C$ is closer to $P$, with $PC=6$. What is $CD$?
problems.hint: The product of the two distances from $P$ to the circle along any line through $P$ is the same for every such line.
problems.solution: The power of $P$ is $PA\cdot PB=5\cdot 12=60$. On the second line, $PC\cdot PD=60$, so $PD=\frac{60}{6}=10$. Hence $CD=PD-PC=10-6=4$.
problems.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
import math
# A circle that realises the data: A=(5,0), B=(12,0) on the x-axis, and P=(0,0)
O = (F(17, 2), F(29, 8))
r2 = (F(5) - O[0])**2 + (F(0) - O[1])**2           # A lies on the circle
assert (F(12) - O[0])**2 + (F(0) - O[1])**2 == r2  # B lies on the circle
power = (O[0]**2 + O[1]**2) - r2                    # power of P
assert power == 60
w = (F(3, 5), F(4, 5))                              # unit direction of second line
wO = w[0]*O[0] + w[1]*O[1]
disc = wO*wO - power                                # points P + s*w on circle: s^2 - 2*wO*s + power = 0
s1 = wO - math.sqrt(disc)
s2 = wO + math.sqrt(disc)
print(round(s2 - s1))

problems.problem: In the coordinate plane, the lines $y=3x$, $y=7-\frac{x}{2}$, and the $x$-axis enclose a triangle. What is the area of this triangle?
problems.hint: Find the three vertices first, by solving the lines in pairs.
problems.solution: The line $y=3x$ meets the $x$-axis at $(0,0)$, and the line $y=7-\frac x2$ meets it at $(14,0)$. The two slanted lines meet where $3x=7-\frac x2$, giving $x=2$ and $y=6$. The base on the $x$-axis has length $14$ and the apex is at height $6$, so the area is $\frac12\cdot 14\cdot 6=42$.
problems.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
def inter(m1, c1, m2, c2):          # intersection of y = m1*x + c1 and y = m2*x + c2
    x = (c2 - c1) / (m1 - m2)
    return (x, m1*x + c1)
P1 = inter(F(3), F(0), F(0), F(0))          # y = 3x meets y = 0
P2 = inter(F(3), F(0), F(-1, 2), F(7))      # y = 3x meets y = 7 - x/2
P3 = inter(F(-1, 2), F(7), F(0), F(0))      # y = 7 - x/2 meets y = 0
pts = [P1, P2, P3]
s = 0
for i in range(3):
    x1, y1 = pts[i]
    x2, y2 = pts[(i + 1) % 3]
    s += x1*y2 - x2*y1
print(F(abs(s), 2))

problems.problem: A solid is formed by attaching a square pyramid to the top face of a cube. The cube has edge length $4$. The base of the pyramid is exactly the top face of the cube, and the apex of the pyramid is $3$ units above that face, directly over its centre. What is the volume of the whole solid?
problems.hint: Add the volume of the cube to the volume of the pyramid, using $V=\frac13 Bh$ for the pyramid.
problems.solution: The cube has volume $4^3=64$. The pyramid has base area $16$ and height $3$, so its volume is $\frac13\cdot 16\cdot 3=16$. The total volume is $64+16=80$.
problems.verify:
# Volume by summing horizontal slices (midpoint rule)
N = 300000
total = 16.0 * 4                        # cube: height 4, cross-section 4 x 4
dz = 3.0 / N
for i in range(N):
    u = (i + 0.5) * dz                  # height above the top face
    total += (4 * (1 - u / 3))**2 * dz  # pyramid slice shrinks linearly to the apex
print(round(total))

problems.problem: Triangle $ABC$ has a right angle at $C$. Let $H$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to the hypotenuse $AB$. Suppose $AH=4$ and $HB=9$. What is the perimeter of triangle $ABC$?
problems.hint: Similar triangles give $AC^2=AH\cdot AB$ and $BC^2=HB\cdot AB$.
problems.solution: The hypotenuse is $AB=4+9=13$. Since $AC^2=AH\cdot AB=4\cdot 13=52$, we get $AC=2\sqrt{13}$. Since $BC^2=HB\cdot AB=9\cdot 13=117$, we get $BC=3\sqrt{13}$. The perimeter is $13+2\sqrt{13}+3\sqrt{13}=13+5\sqrt{13}$.
problems.verify:
import math
A = (-4, 0); B = (9, 0); C = (0, 6)     # H = (0,0) is the foot of the altitude
def d(P, Q):
    return math.hypot(P[0] - Q[0], P[1] - Q[1])
assert (A[0] - C[0])*(B[0] - C[0]) + (A[1] - C[1])*(B[1] - C[1]) == 0   # right angle at C
perim = d(A, B) + d(B, C) + d(C, A)
assert abs(perim - (13 + 5*math.sqrt(13))) < 1e-9
print("13+5\\sqrt{13}")

problems.problem: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $5$. A chord $AB$ of the circle has length $8$. The chord is extended past $B$ to a point $P$ with $BP=4$. A tangent from $P$ touches the circle at $T$. What is $PT$?
problems.hint: Power of a point: the square of a tangent equals the product of the two segments of a secant from $P$.
problems.solution: Here $PA=AB+BP=12$ and $PB=4$, so $PT^2=PA\cdot PB=48$, giving $PT=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt{3}$. The radius is not needed for the calculation; it only fixes the picture.
problems.verify:
import math
O = (0, 0); r = 5
A = (-4, 3); B = (4, 3); P = (8, 3)     # chord AB is 8 long and P is 4 past B
for X in (A, B):
    assert abs(math.hypot(X[0] - O[0], X[1] - O[1]) - r) < 1e-9
assert abs(math.hypot(B[0] - A[0], B[1] - A[1]) - 8) < 1e-9
PT = math.sqrt((P[0] - O[0])**2 + (P[1] - O[1])**2 - r*r)   # tangent length from P
assert abs(PT - 4*math.sqrt(3)) < 1e-9
print("4\\sqrt{3}")

problems.problem: Let $P=(1,7)$, and let $Q$ be the reflection of $P$ across the line $y=x-1$. What is the area of the triangle with vertices $O=(0,0)$, $P$, and $Q$?
problems.hint: Segment $PQ$ is perpendicular to the mirror line, and its midpoint lies on the mirror line.
problems.solution: Write $Q=(1+t,\,7-t)$, which moves in the direction $(1,-1)$ perpendicular to the line. The midpoint $\left(1+\frac t2,\,7-\frac t2\right)$ must lie on $y=x-1$, so $7-\frac t2=\frac t2$, giving $t=7$ and $Q=(8,0)$. The area of $OPQ$ is $\frac12\left|1\cdot 0-8\cdot 7\right|=28$.
problems.verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
P = (F(1), F(7))
a, b, c = F(1), F(-1), F(-1)              # mirror line x - y - 1 = 0, i.e. y = x - 1
k = (a*P[0] + b*P[1] + c) / (a*a + b*b)
Q = (P[0] - 2*k*a, P[1] - 2*k*b)          # standard reflection formula
M = ((P[0] + Q[0]) / 2, (P[1] + Q[1]) / 2)
assert a*M[0] + b*M[1] + c == 0           # midpoint lies on the mirror
assert (Q[0] - P[0])*b - (Q[1] - P[1])*a == 0   # PQ is parallel to the normal (a, b)
print(F(abs(P[0]*Q[1] - Q[0]*P[1]), 2))  # shoelace area of O, P, Q

problems.problem: A right circular cone has base radius $6$ and height $8$, with its apex at the top. A sphere is placed inside the cone so that it touches the flat base and the curved lateral surface all the way around. What is the radius of the sphere?
problems.hint: Look at the cross-section through the axis. It is an isosceles triangle, and the sphere's cross-section is a circle inside it.
problems.solution: The axial cross-section is an isosceles triangle with base $12$ and height $8$, so its sides are $10$, $10$, $12$. The sphere's centre lies on the axis at height $r$, and it is at distance $r$ from the slanted sides, so the sphere's cross-section is the incircle of this triangle. Its radius is $r=\frac{K}{s}$, where $K=\frac12\cdot 12\cdot 8=48$ and $s=\frac{10+10+12}{2}=16$. So $r=\frac{48}{16}=3$.

problems.problem: Point $P$ lies inside rectangle $ABCD$. Its distances to three of the vertices are $PA=3$, $PB=4$, and $PC=5$. What is $PD$?
problems.hint: For a point inside a rectangle, the sums of squared distances to two opposite corners are equal for both pairs of opposite corners.
problems.solution: This is the rectangle identity $PA^2+PC^2=PB^2+PD^2$, which holds for every point inside a rectangle. So $9+25=16+PD^2$, giving $PD^2=18$ and $PD=3\sqrt{2}$. To see why, put $A$ at the origin with the sides along the axes and add up the squared coordinate gaps for each pair of opposite corners.
problems.verify:
import math
# Build a rectangle A=(0,0), B=(w,0), C=(w,h), D=(0,h) and a point P=(x,y) with PA=3, PB=4, PC=5
x = 1.0; y = math.sqrt(8.0)
w = x + math.sqrt(16 - y*y)                 # PB = 4
h = y + math.sqrt(25 - (w - x)**2)          # PC = 5
PA = math.hypot(x, y)
PB = math.hypot(w - x, y)
PC = math.hypot(w - x, h - y)
assert abs(PA - 3) < 1e-9 and abs(PB - 4) < 1e-9 and abs(PC - 5) < 1e-9
assert 0 < x < w and 0 < y < h             # P is inside the rectangle
PD = math.hypot(x, h - y)                   # D = (0, h)
assert abs(PD - 3*math.sqrt(2)) < 1e-9
print("3\\sqrt{2}")
